title: Meatloaf
ingredients: 1 lb ground beef (the family version uses 3 lbs — see notes)
2 eggs, beaten first — both, even for the 1 lb version
method: Heat the oven to 350°F.
Beat the eggs before anything else goes in.
Chop the onion and celery. They go in raw.
Mix everything together — the ketchup and mustard go into the mix.
Shape into a loaf, either in a loaf pan or free-form on a tray.
Bake for 1 hour.

notes.text: The family version: 3 lbs of beef, and ketchup spread on top before it goes in the oven. This version is 1 lb and no ketchup on top.
The hour at 350°F is the real time for the 1 lb version — that's the one that actually gets made. No time was recorded for the 3 lb family version, which will need longer.
If you ever make the 3 lb size, 160°F in the middle is the doneness check.
Loaf pan or free-form both work.
Free-form gives you more crust; a pan means it sits in its own fat.
The onion, celery, breadcrumbs and garlic powder are eyeballed, not measured. That's how it's made, not a detail that went missing.
Both eggs go in even with 1 lb of beef. Whether the 3 lb family version scales the eggs up isn't known.

title: Roasted Potatoes
ingredients: Potatoes — peeled, or red potatoes with the skins left on
method: Cut the potatoes into bite-size cubes.
Spread on a tray and toss with olive oil, garlic powder, salt and pepper.
Roast at 350°F for 20 minutes.

notes.text: Temperature confirmed at 350°F by the family member who makes these. It wasn't written on the original recipe.
Bite-size cubes, as best remembered, rather than a recorded instruction.
Small cubes in a single layer cook far faster than chunks, which makes 20 minutes at 350°F plausible — though still brisk, so check with a fork rather than trusting the clock.
For contrast, Roasted Veggies gives potatoes 45 minutes at 400°F. Probably no conflict — that one likely means larger pieces.

title: American Spaghetti and Meatballs
ingredients: 1 box of pasta — normally angel hair
1 egg — the only binder, no breadcrumbs
Tomato soup — enough to fill the pot, made up as normal soup (if condensed, add water per the can)
American cheese, or Velveeta — about half a block of Velveeta, melted in
method: In a pot, make up the tomato soup as normal soup — if it's condensed, add the water the can calls for. Melt the American cheese or Velveeta into it.
Mix the ground beef with the egg, salt, pepper and celery salt or celery seed. No breadcrumbs.
Roll into meatballs.
Drop the raw meatballs into the soup and cheese mixture and cook them in it.
Boil the pasta.
Serve the meatballs and sauce over the pasta.

notes.text: No breadcrumbs — deliberate, not an omission. The egg is the only binder.
The meatballs go in raw and cook in the sauce. They're never browned.
Quantities are by feel rather than measured. What typically gets used: a pound of ground beef, enough soup to fill the pot, and around half a block of Velveeta melted in.
The pasta isn't named in the original — it's normally angel hair, a whole box.
This is the tomato-soup-and-melted-cheese style rather than an Italian red sauce. Worth saying so it doesn't get 'corrected' into marinara.
Cooking the meatballs in the sauce means the sauce takes on flavor from the beef.
Raw meatballs are fragile until they've set, so leave them alone for the first few minutes rather than stirring.

title: Sour Cucumbers
time: Half an hour soaking, then a few minutes
method: Slice the cucumbers.
Soak the slices in salt water for half an hour.
Tip into a colander and squeeze really tight to get the water out.
Slice the onions into half-moons.
Mix the cucumbers and onions with sour cream, salt and pepper.

notes.text: No vinegar — checked, not an omission. The sour comes from the sour cream.
Slice, soak in salt water for half an hour, then squeeze really tight. Both steps matter.
The salting and squeezing pull water out of the cucumbers, which is what keeps the sour cream thick instead of turning into a puddle. Squeeze harder than feels reasonable.
The onion cut isn't certain — half-moon slices is the best recollection, not a recorded instruction.
Thin either way: raw onion goes strong in sour cream when the pieces are big.
Quantities are eyeballed — cucumbers, onion and sour cream all to taste. There are no measures for this one.

title: Three-Ingredient Peanut Butter Cookies
from: several recipe sites — the standard three-ingredient version
blurb: Three ingredients, no flour, and done in about ten minutes.
method: Heat the oven to 350°F.
Mix the peanut butter, sugar and egg together until smooth.
Roll into balls and space them out on a baking sheet.
Press a criss-cross pattern into each one with a fork.
Bake for 10 minutes.

notes.text: Coconut sugar works in place of white sugar — both are in the original.
No flour at all, so these happen to be gluten-free as long as the peanut butter is.
The fork criss-cross isn't only decoration — it flattens the balls so they bake through evenly in the 10 minutes.
They come out very soft and firm up as they cool, so don't judge them straight from the oven.

title: Plain White Rice
method: In a semi-shallow pan on high heat, mix the oil, salt and rice. Mix until the rice is coated with the oil, then add the water.

Flatten the rice. You have the right amount of water when the tip of the spoon is submerged about one inch, measured from the top of the rice mound. Make sure the spoon is resting on top of the rice, NOT on the bottom of the pan.
Low to medium heat, and keep an eye on it until the water is gone.
Mix again, drop the heat to low, and cover with a tight lid.
After 20 minutes it should be ready to fold — the part that was on top flips to the bottom, and so on.
Cover again and give it another 10 to 20 minutes. If you want thicker concón, leave it longer.
troubleshooting: If when you uncover the rice after the first 20 minutes the grains look too closed (uncooked), sprinkle with water, mix, and cover again.

variations.name: Thicker, crunchier concón
variations.how: Add the oil to the hot pan, followed by the water. Once the water boils, add the salt and rice. Then proceed with the same steps.

variations.name: Rice and corn, or any other vegetable
variations.how: Cook the rice as above. Sauté the vegetables separately with the seasoning you want, then mix with the rice and serve.

notes.text: The spoon test is the real measurement — the 3 cups of water is approximate, and the spoon is what actually tells you.
At 20 minutes the rice is folded, not stirred: the part that was on top goes to the bottom.
Folding rather than stirring gives both layers time against the pan, which is where the concón comes from.

title: Roasted Chicken
time: An hour and a half at 450°F
ingredients: A pinch of hot pepper flakes
method: In a small blender, mix the garlic, the juice of the lemon (reserve the wedges), rosemary, olive oil, salt, pepper and hot pepper flakes. Blend well.
Melt the butter and add it to the mixture.
Clean the chicken, removing the fat around the neck and the bottom.
Cover the chicken with the sauce, including the empty cavity.
Place the lemon wedges inside the cavity.
Roast at 450°F for an hour and a half. Turn the chicken once it is golden on top, so the color and texture come out even. Finish roasting.

variations.name: Chicken pieces instead of a whole bird
variations.how: You can do the same with chicken pieces. It takes less time.

notes.text: The pepper flakes here are dried chile de árbol, ground in the blender. Sold at Giant Eagle and Walmart.
Reserve the lemon wedges when you juice it — they go in the cavity, they aren't a garnish.
Chicken sizes vary a lot, so the hour and a half shifts with the bird. The thickest part of the thigh reaching 165°F is the reliable check.

title: Dominican Beans
time: All day or overnight for the beans, then simmered until creamy
ingredients: Dry beans — red Dominican, pinto, or cranberry. Stay away from kidney beans, they don't make any sauce. About 2 to 3 cups, or the small bag from the grocery store
1 cubanelle or bell pepper, cut in half, seeds removed
8 garlic cloves, mashed (or ¼ cup Dominican sazón)
1 handful of cilantro — do NOT cut it
method: In a slow cooker, rinse and cook the dry beans with double the water — so for 2 cups of beans, 4 cups of water. Cook on slow during the day, or overnight if you are an early riser.
The beans are ready when you squeeze one and the cream inside comes right out.
In a deep pan on high heat, mix all the ingredients except the beans. Mix well until the mixture is nice and hot and the tomato paste is mixed in.
Add the beans with their liquid. Mix well, and add more water if the liquid is too low.
Let it boil, then drop the heat to medium-low. At this point you can add the habanero whole — it will be easy to remove later.
Stir occasionally. Taste for salt and pepper. The beans are ready once they are medium thick and creamy.
Remove all the vegetables before serving.

notes.text: The pepper and onion go in only halved and the cilantro isn't cut, and step 7 takes all the vegetables back out before serving. They're there to flavor the pot, not to be eaten in it.
The habanero goes in whole so it's easy to remove later — that's how the heat is controlled.
Beans will be creamier if they cook slowly.
The squeeze test is the doneness check for the beans, not the clock — the cream should come straight out.
¼ cup of Dominican Sazón stands in for the 8 garlic cloves if you have it.

title: Dominican Sazón
serves: About a big mason jar — roughly a quart
blurb: The seasoning base the other Dominican recipes call for.
ingredients: A handful of freshly ground pepper
method: In a regular-size blender, blend everything together.

notes.text: It needs to be refrigerated, and is best used within a week or two.
Yield is about a big mason jar, roughly a quart — near enough what a standard blender holds. Approximate rather than measured.
¼ cup of this stands in for the 8 garlic cloves in Dominican Beans.
If a whole jar is more than you'll get through in a week or two, freezing part of it in portions is worth considering.

title: Roasted Veggies
method: Spread olive oil on a tray.
Add the cut vegetables.
Sprinkle with salt, pepper and hot pepper flakes.
Roast at 400°F until nice and tender — anywhere from 20 to 45 minutes depending on the vegetables. Potatoes, sweet potatoes and the like will be 45 minutes.

notes.text: The oil goes on the tray first, then the vegetables on top of it.
The 20-to-45-minute range isn't vagueness, it's the instruction — potatoes and sweet potatoes take the full 45. Judge by tender, not by clock.
Generalizing from that: the denser the vegetable, the closer to 45 minutes; softer ones nearer 20.
The recipe just says 'hot pepper flakes'. It's probably the same ground dried chile de árbol as in the Roasted Chicken, given the same kitchen — but that's an assumption, not stated.

title: Mangú
method: Peel and cut the plantains, and boil them with salt.
Watch for the color change — the plantains turn a dark yellow, and if they're green the water takes on a purple-grayish color. At this point, add cold water.
Remove from the heat when they are soft when pinched with a fork.
Remove almost all the water, leaving about ¼ cup in with the plantains for easy mashing.
Add butter and milk, and mash until nice and creamy.
Serve immediately — the mangú will go hard once it cools off.
troubleshooting: If it has gone hard from cooling, heat it in the microwave, add more fat or cheese, and mash again.

notes.text: Filed under Breakfast because that's what it is, but in practice it gets eaten more as a side — and often as breakfast for dinner.
The cold water goes in at the color change, not at the start. It's a step in its own right, not topping up the pot.
The color is the timer. Dark yellow plantains, or purple-grayish water if you started with green ones.
Don't drain it dry — the ¼ cup of cooking water left behind is what lets it mash creamy.
Serve immediately is an instruction, not a suggestion. It goes hard as it cools.

title: Pie Crust
blurb: The last pie crust you'll ever need.
ingredients: ½ cup flour (separate — for the slurry)
method: Blend the 1½ cups of flour and the 2 sticks of butter together with a pastry blender.
Separately, mix the ½ cup of flour with the ½ cup of water to make a slurry.
Add the slurry to the butter and flour, and add the salt.
Mix together with your hands or a spoon.
Take it out and knead until it forms a ball.
Divide in half. Makes 2 crusts.

notes.text: The flour is listed twice on purpose. 1½ cups goes into the butter; a separate ½ cup makes the slurry. It isn't a duplication.
Combining the two lots of flour would give you a different pastry — the slurry is the method.
It rolls easier when refrigerated, but it bakes the same either way.
Passed along by the same person the Dominican recipes came from, who had it from Mrs. L. The original is titled "The Last Pie Crust you'll ever need."

title: Dominican Flan de Leche
time: 2 hours or more in the oven, then 12 to 24 hours in the fridge

items: 3 tablespoons of a good golden rum

method: In a deep small pan over medium heat, heat the sugar and vanilla. Stir occasionally so it won't burn.
Once the caramel is ready it should look soft and liquid. Pour it into the baking dish, coating the bottom and the sides. Set aside.
In a blender, mix the rest of the ingredients until smooth — about 2 minutes.
Pour into the baking dish, the one with the caramel.
Bake it using the Bain Marie method — the baking dish sitting inside a larger dish of hot water. Any other method will harden the mix — you will get dulce de leche, not flan.
Place in the oven at 325°F for two hours or more. It's ready when a toothpick comes out clean.
Let it cool off a little before putting it in the fridge for the next 12 to 24 hours.
To serve, pass a knife around the edges and put a serving dish on top. Turn it over — it should fall onto the plate.

notes.text: The Bain Marie isn't a preference. The recipe is explicit: any other method gives you dulce de leche instead of flan.
The 12 to 24 hours in the fridge is part of making it, not storage — the recipe separately says it keeps up to a week after that.
Full fat is specified for both the evaporated and the condensed milk.

title: Morir Soñando
blurb: Orange juice and evaporated milk, blended cold.
ingredients: ⅓ cup of sugar — more or less, depending on how sweet you like it
method: In a blender, mix together the orange juice, sugar and ice. Blend until nice and smooth.
With the blender still running, add the evaporated milk slowly.
Serve cold.

variations.name: Condensed milk instead of sugar
variations.how: Some people substitute the sugar for 1 can of condensed milk.

notes.text: Yes, it is called Morir Soñando — dying in your dreams.
The milk goes in slowly with the blender still running.
That slow pour is what stops it splitting — orange juice is acidic enough to curdle milk if the two meet all at once, and keeping everything cold helps too.
The sugar is to taste rather than a fixed amount.

title: Southern Style Chicken and Doughballs
time: 1½ hours for the broth, then 15–20 minutes
blurb: Also known as Elmer's Glue, because it sticks to your ribs.

items: Water — 1 to 2 inches over the chicken
3 cups flour (2¾ may be enough — see notes)
1 cup chicken broth, from the pot
soup base — possibly a bouillon cube, see notes

method: Put the whole chicken in a big pot with the garlic, celery, onions, carrots, soup base, salt and pepper.
Add water to come 1 or 2 inches over the chicken.
Boil, then simmer with the lid on for 1½ hours.
Strain. You should have about 6 cups of broth.
For the doughballs: melt the margarine, then add the salt, parsley and flour.
Add 1 cup of the chicken broth and mix to a dough.
Roll to ⅛ inch on a floured surface, and cut into 2 inch squares.
Get the broth boiling — it must be boiling before the doughballs go in, or they stick together.
Add the doughballs and simmer for 15 to 20 minutes, until tender.
troubleshooting: Too sticky, add flour. Too floury, add broth.

notes.text: Elmer's Glue is what GiGi called it, because it sticks to your ribs.
The card says 3 cups of flour with "2¾" written beside it. You may not need the full 3 — go by the dough, and the too sticky / too floury note below.
Serve mashed potatoes alongside, as a side rather than in the pot.
The card writes "tsp salt" with no number — 1 tsp is the best guess rather than a recorded amount, and the soup base has no quantity at all.
The soup base may have been one of those soup cubes rather than a paste or powder, but that isn't certain.

title: Cherry Nut Bread
blurb: A vintage quick bread with maraschino cherries and walnuts.
ingredients: Milk — enough to make the cherry juice up to 1 cup
½ cup walnuts, or other nuts
method: Heat the oven to 350°F and grease an 8x4 inch loaf pan.
Cream the butter and brown sugar together until light, then beat in the egg.
In a separate bowl, whisk the flour, baking powder and salt together.
Drain the juice from the cherries into a measuring cup, then top it up with milk until you have 1 cup of liquid.
Add the flour mixture and the cherry milk to the butter mixture in turns, stirring only until it comes together.
Chop the cherries, then fold them and the walnuts through the batter.
Pour into the pan and bake for 45 to 60 minutes, until a toothpick comes out clean.
Cool in the pan for 10 minutes, then turn out onto a wire rack to cool completely.

notes.text: Don't throw the cherry juice away — it makes up part of the 1 cup of liquid, and it's where the color and most of the cherry flavor come from.
Stir only until it comes together. Overworking a quick bread batter makes the loaf tough.

title: Twice-Baked Potatoes
method: Bake the potatoes at 350°F for 1 hour.
Cut each one in half and scoop out the inside.
Mash the potato on low until there are no lumps, adding the milk a little at a time until it's smooth.
Add the butter, salt and pepper.
Stir in the cheese and the chives or green onions.
Fill the shells with the mixture and set them on a sheet.
Bake at 400°F for 20 minutes.

notes.text: The bacon is optional and doesn't appear in the steps on the card. Cook it separately and put it on top rather than mixing it through.
Where this one came from isn't known.

title: Pumpkin Quick Bread
time: 60 to 70 minutes at 350°F, plus an hour cooling
method: Preheat the oven to 350°F.
Line a 9x5 pan with parchment paper.
Whisk the wet ingredients together. Whisk the dry ingredients together separately.
Fold the wet into the dry ingredients.
Bake for 60 to 70 minutes.
Let it cool for 1 hour before removing it from the pan.

notes.text: The card groups the ingredients into wet and dry with a gap between them, and the method whisks each separately before folding — so the two lists are part of the instruction, not just layout.
The full hour of cooling before you take it out of the pan is on the card. A quick bread this wet will tear if you rush it.
Found online somewhere — the exact source wasn't recorded.

title: Apple Fritters
from: a cooking show — possibly America's Test Kitchen
time: 2 to 3 minutes a side, plus 10 minutes for the glaze

items: 2 apples, cut into ¼ inch pieces and patted dry — do not grate them

method: Cut the apples into ¼ inch pieces — don't grate them — and pat them dry.
Mix the dry ingredients together.
Toss the apple pieces through the dry mixture.
Whisk the wet ingredients together, then combine with the dry until no flour is left.
In a deep pot, heat 3 cups of oil over medium-high heat.
Scoop ⅓ cup portions into the oil, 5 at a time, and press them down. Fry for 2 to 3 minutes a side.
Lift out and cool for 5 minutes.
For the glaze, whisk the powdered sugar, cider, cinnamon and nutmeg together.
Let the glaze sit on the fritters for 10 minutes before eating.

notes.text: Don't grate the apples — ¼ inch pieces, patted dry. The recipe is emphatic about it.
Grated apple releases its water into the batter, which makes the fritters soggy and stops them holding shape. Cut pieces keep their texture.
The apples get tossed in the dry mixture before the wet goes in, so every piece is floured before it meets the batter.
Copied down while watching a cooking show. Which show wasn't recorded — America's Test Kitchen is the best guess.
The unit on the ¾ apple cider wasn't written down. Cup is the reading, and it fits against 2 cups of flour.

title: Amaretto Sour
method: Combine the amaretto and sweet & sour.
Shake vigorously to aerate it — the foam enhances the flavor.
Serve over ice.

notes.text: The vigorous shake isn't optional. The foam it produces is part of the drink, not just how it looks.
It's 1 part amaretto to 2 parts sweet & sour, so it scales straight up for a pitcher.
A sour with orange juice in it is called a stone sour, so the amaretto stone sour name is the real one.

variations.name: Blended instead of shaken
variations.how: Put it in a blender rather than shaking. It aerates far more than a shaker can, and you get a lot more foam.

variations.name: Amaretto Stone Sour
variations.how: Add orange juice to the amaretto and sweet & sour.

title: Russian Tea Cakes
method: Preheat the oven to 350°F.
Cream the butter and vanilla together.
Combine the 6 tbsp of confectioners sugar with the flour.
Stir that into the butter mixture until blended.
Mix in the walnuts.
Roll into balls on an ungreased sheet.
Bake for 12 minutes.
When cool, roll them in confectioners sugar — maybe twice.

notes.text: The confectioners sugar appears twice for different jobs: 6 tbsp goes into the dough with the flour, and ⅓ cup is for rolling the baked cookies. Not a duplication.
"Maybe twice" on the final rolling is what the card says — roll them once when cool, then again if they need it.
Where this one came from isn't known — probably found online somewhere.

title: Orange/Lemon Cookies

items: 1 cup sour milk — 2 tbsp vinegar plus 1 cup milk
Juice of 1 orange, plus the rind
Juice of an orange, plus the rind

methodNote: The card gives the ingredients, the oven temperature, the bake time and the parchment paper — but no mixing steps. The order below is a standard reconstruction, not what was written down.
method: Heat the oven to 350°F and line a sheet with parchment paper.
Make the sour milk: stir the 2 tbsp of vinegar into the cup of milk.
Cream the margarine and sugar together, then beat in the eggs.
Whisk the flour, baking powder and baking soda together separately.
Add the dry ingredients and the sour milk to the creamed mixture in turns, mixing just until combined.
Stir in the orange juice and rind.
Drop spoonfuls onto the lined sheet.
Bake for 12 to 15 minutes.
For the icing, melt the butter and mix it into the confectioners sugar, adding orange juice and rind until it spreads. Ice the cookies once they're cool.

notes.text: Sour milk isn't something you buy — 2 tbsp of vinegar stirred into a cup of milk is what the card means.
The title offers a choice: the ingredients only name orange, so lemon is presumably the alternative rather than a second citrus.
The bake temperature, the time and the parchment paper are all from the card. Only the order of mixing is mine.
The icing is made by melting the butter and mixing it into the sugar, rather than beating in softened butter.

title: Slow Cooker Cheeseburger Soup
ingredients: 4 large potatoes, cubed — peeled if you'd rather not eat the peels
1 teaspoon fine sea salt, plus more to taste
method: Brown the ground beef in a large skillet, then add the onion and garlic and cook until the onion softens.
Sprinkle the flour over it and keep cooking and stirring for 3 to 5 minutes, until the flour browns.
Tip that into the slow cooker, then add the potatoes, carrots, dried parsley, salt, pepper and chicken stock.
Cook on low for 4 to 6 hours.
Half an hour before serving, stir in the milk and the cheese and let it warm through. Taste, and add more salt and pepper.
Garnish with fresh parsley if you like, and serve right away.

notes.text: Originally Slow Cooker Cheeseburger Soup from The Prairie Homestead, and it came to you through the Dominican family.
The handwritten card in the box has only nine ingredients and no method — it's missing the parsley, salt, pepper and onion powder, and gives no hint that it's a slow cooker recipe at all.
The onion powder is in the ingredient list but never appears in the steps. Adding it with the other seasonings is the obvious place, but the original doesn't say so.
Browning the flour for 3 to 5 minutes is a real step, not just thickening — it's what stops the soup tasting of raw flour.

title: Sacher Torte
time: About 45 minutes to bake, plus cooling and assembly
blurb: Chocolate cake layered with apricot and finished with a poured chocolate glaze.

items: ¼ cup plus 2 teaspoons confectioners' sugar
½ cup plus 2 tablespoons white sugar
3 tablespoons dark rum, divided — 2 tbsp for the syrup, 1 tbsp for the apricot

method: Heat the oven to 350°F. Grease a 9-inch springform pan, line the base with a circle of parchment, and grease the paper too.
Melt the 4 ounces of chocolate in a double boiler over simmering water, stirring often and scraping the sides so it doesn't scorch — 3 to 5 minutes. Off the heat, let it cool for 5 to 10 minutes.
Beat the butter with the confectioners' sugar until creamy. Mix in the melted chocolate, then beat in the egg yolks one at a time.
In a glass bowl, beat the egg whites until foamy. Add the white sugar gradually and keep beating to stiff, glossy peaks.
Fold the whites into the chocolate mixture, then fold in the cake flour until it's incorporated.
Pour into the pan, smooth the top, and bake about 45 minutes — the edges pull away from the sides and a toothpick comes out dry.
Cool in the pan on a wire rack for 15 minutes. Run a small knife around the edge, release the sides, and let it cool completely on the base — another 15 to 20 minutes.
For the syrup, boil the ¼ cup of water with the ¼ cup of sugar until it's clear, 2 to 3 minutes. Off the heat, stir in 2 tablespoons of the rum.
For the apricot, blend the preserves with 1 tablespoon of water until smooth. Simmer in a saucepan until thickened, about 2 minutes, then stir in the last tablespoon of rum.
Take the pan base and parchment off the cooled cake, and slice it horizontally into two layers.
Set the bottom layer on a wire rack. Brush a third of the syrup over it, spread on a third of the apricot purée, and put the other layer on top.
Brush the rest of the syrup over the top and sides, then spread the remaining purée over the top and sides. Chill it on the rack while you make the icing.
For the icing, melt the 9 ounces of chocolate in a double boiler, stirring and scraping, 3 to 5 minutes. Let it cool slightly.
Bring the cream to a simmer and stir it into the melted chocolate. Let it cool, stirring often, until it's spreadable — 5 to 10 minutes.
Set the rack over waxed paper to catch drips. Pour the icing over the cake and spread it across the top and sides, letting the excess run through the rack.
Let the icing come to room temperature, then move the cake to a platter. Serve at room temperature.

notes.text: A special occasion cake rather than an everyday one.
The rum is divided: 2 tablespoons go into the syrup, the last tablespoon into the apricot purée.
Both sugars are listed in two parts on the original — ¼ cup plus 2 teaspoons of confectioners', and ½ cup plus 2 tablespoons of white. They're used together, so they're combined here.
The wire rack sits over waxed paper for the glazing so the excess can run off. Trying to glaze it on a plate won't work.

title: No Bake Chocolate & Peanut Butter Oat Bars
time: 30 minutes, plus 2 to 3 hours in the fridge
blurb: No oven — an oat base, a chocolate peanut butter layer, and oats crumbled over the top.
ingredients: ½ cup creamy peanut butter — 100% peanuts, no sugar added
method: Grease a 9x13 inch casserole dish. A smaller pan — 8x8 or similar — gives you thicker bars.
Melt the butter in a large saucepan over medium heat. Stir in the coconut sugar and vanilla, then mix in the oats. Cook over low heat for 2 to 3 minutes, until everything is well blended.
Press half the oat mixture into the bottom of the pan, and keep the other half back for the top.
In a small heavy saucepan over low heat, melt the chocolate chips and peanut butter together, stirring often until smooth.
Pour the chocolate mixture over the crust and spread it evenly.
Crumble the remaining oat mixture over the chocolate and press it in gently.
Cover and refrigerate for 2 to 3 hours, until the chocolate hardens.
Bring it back to room temperature before cutting into bars.

notes.text: Reached you by email, having passed through several people before it got to you.
The salted butter is the only salt in the recipe. Unsalted would flatten it.

100% peanuts with no added sugar matters here rather than being a preference — a sweetened peanut butter would tip the bars over, since the coconut sugar and a cup of chocolate chips are already doing that.
The same oat mixture does two jobs: half pressed down as the base, half crumbled over the top. Don't cook two batches.
Cutting it straight from the fridge will crack the chocolate — that's why it comes back to room temperature first.

If you want it exactly as the sender makes it, their brands were Kerrygold salted butter, Madhava coconut sugar, McCormick vanilla, Quaker 1-minute oats, Ghirardelli chips and Krema peanut butter — all from Walmart.

The email cites an AllRecipes recipe called No-Bake Chocolate Oat Bars, but this version has peanut butter in the title and uses coconut sugar — so it has almost certainly picked up changes along the way. Treat this as the version that was passed to you rather than the original.

title: Tart Cranberry Punch
blurb: A party-sized punch, with a fruit ice ring to keep it cold.

items: 4 bottles (3 liter) 100% cranberry juice — about 48 cups
5 cans frozen lemonade, thawed — see notes

method: In a large bowl, combine 1 bottle of cranberry juice, 1½ cans of thawed lemonade and 1 liter of 7-Up — half a bottle.
Stir, and pour into a 1-gallon jug. There'll be some left over.
Repeat until you have 4 to 4½ gallons of punch.
For the ice ring, arrange the lemon slices, raspberries and mint in the bottom of an ice ring mold or a bundt pan.
Add just enough water to submerge about a third of the lemon slices, and freeze for 20 minutes, or until hard.
Top up with enough water to make a substantial ring, around 4 inches thick, and freeze until hard.

notes.text: Found in an email about a get-together. Where it came from before that isn't known.

CHECK: the numbers don't quite divide. Each gallon takes 1½ cans of lemonade, so four gallons needs 6 cans — but the ingredient list says 5. Either buy 6, or the per-batch amount is meant to be lower. Worth settling before shopping for a party.
The ice ring freezes in two stages on purpose. A shallow layer first anchors the fruit in place; add all the water at once and the lemon and raspberries float to the top.
An ice ring rather than cubes because it melts far more slowly, so the punch stays cold without watering down as fast.

title: Almond Flour Cocoa Bread
ingredients: 1¼ cups apple sauce, pumpkin purée, or mashed banana
¼ cup brown sugar or coconut sugar
½ cup dark chocolate chips, plus extra for the top
method: Heat the oven to 350°F. Spray a loaf pan with cooking spray, or line it with parchment, and set it aside.
In a large bowl, mash the bananas — or use apple sauce or pumpkin purée. Add the eggs, maple syrup, brown or coconut sugar, and vanilla, and whisk until smooth and well combined.
Add the almond flour, cocoa powder, baking soda and salt to the same bowl. With a wooden spoon or spatula, gently fold everything together until just combined.
Fold in ½ cup of the chocolate chips, spread evenly through the batter.
Pour into the pan and smooth the top with a spatula.
Scatter the remaining chocolate chips over the top.
Bake for 55 minutes to an hour, until a toothpick comes out mostly clean from the center.
Let it cool for 10 minutes before removing, then transfer to a wire rack to cool completely.
Cut and serve.

notes.text: Passed on by someone you stayed with. Not made yet — it's here so it doesn't get lost in an inbox.
The sugar is missing from the recipe card's steps, but the article body puts it in with the eggs, maple syrup and vanilla. That's where it goes.

The card says "mix well" for the dry ingredients; the article says gently fold until just combined. The gentler instruction is the one to follow — almond flour has no gluten to develop, but overworking still knocks the air out.
It's a one-bowl recipe. The dry ingredients go into the same bowl as the wet, so don't set up a second one.
A toothpick coming out "mostly clean" is what the recipe asks for, not clean. Almond flour loaves stay moist, and baking until a toothpick is dry will overcook it.
The 1¼ cups is a choice of three — apple sauce, pumpkin, or mashed banana. They'll all work, but the loaf tastes noticeably different depending on which.
